questions.lead_in: What type of outbreak is represented in the epidemic curve?
questions.explanation: Propagated progressive source An epidemic curve is a visual display of the onset of illness during an outbreak. Point source epidemics involve a common source and occur over a brief period. Common persistent courses rise and fall, but the cases do not occur within a single incubation period. Propagated progressive sources occur when there is an initial wave of infections followed by second or third waves. There are successively larger peaks. Intermittent outbreaks are separated by periods without evidence of infection.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) MRSA bacteraemia and invasive infection carry higher attributable mortality than methicillin-susceptible S. aureus. (2) Colonization leads to subsequent infection with increased morbidity, longer length of stay and need for second-line agents (vancomycin) with more toxicity/failure. (3) Substantial excess healthcare cost, and colonized patients act as a reservoir seeding further nosocomial spread/outbreaks.
b) (1) Hand hygiene with alcohol-based hand rub at the point of care. (2) Contact precautions with gown and gloves in a single room, or cohorting of colonized/infected patients. (4) Enhanced environmental cleaning and disinfection of the room and shared/reusable equipment (dedicated equipment where possible). (5) Decolonization of selected patients (nasal mupirocin plus chlorhexidine bathing, e.g. preoperatively or in ICU). (6) Antimicrobial stewardship to reduce selective pressure, supported by surveillance, feedback of MRSA rates and staff education; minimize intra-facility patient movement.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Fit — successful quantitative/qualitative fit testing to the specific make, model and size, since face shape, weight change, and facial hair (beard) cause leak. (2) Seal check — the wearer performing a user seal check every time the respirator is donned, and the absence of anything crossing the seal (glasses straps, hair). (3) Correct and consistent use — worn for the entire exposure, not touched or repositioned, straps placed properly, removed and discarded when wet, soiled or damaged, with hand hygiene. (4) Product/programmatic factors — a NIOSH-certified N95 that is not counterfeit or damaged, used within a complete respiratory protection program (training, medical clearance, and the right respirator for the hazard — PAPR for very high-risk aerosol-generating procedures).

questions.question_raw: Nosocomial MRSA Infections

parts.text: List 3 reasons why it is important to prevent hospital transmission of MRSA.
List 6 strategies of an MRSA prevention program.

parts_raw.text: List 3 reasons why it's important to prevent hospital transmission of MRSA.
List 6 strategies of an MRSA prevention program.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) MRSA infection carries higher attributable morbidity and mortality than MSSA infection. (2) It prolongs length of stay and markedly increases cost of care, including isolation. (3) Colonization persists and predisposes to later invasive infection and to onward transmission, and mandates use of more toxic/less effective second-line agents (vancomycin, linezolid, daptomycin).
b) (1) Perform a facility MRSA risk assessment and set measurable reduction targets. (2) Conduct MRSA surveillance, including targeted admission screening of high-risk patients and a laboratory-based alert system flagging new and readmitted/transferred MRSA patients. (3) Optimize hand hygiene compliance with audit and feedback. (4) Apply contact precautions (gown and gloves, single room or cohorting) to colonized and infected patients. (5) Ensure adequate environmental cleaning/disinfection and dedicated or disinfected patient equipment. (6) Educate healthcare personnel, patients and families; add antimicrobial stewardship, decolonization where indicated (e.g. preoperative, recurrent infection) and insertion/maintenance bundles for devices and surgery.
questions.beyond_mandell: SHEA/IDSA Compendium MRSA prevention; PHAC MRSA guidance.

cohort_answer.text: Reasons: MRSA infections have higher morbidity/mortality (~2x) and longer hospital stays/cost vs MSSA; once colonized, high risk of recurrent infections (39% within 18 months); infection control costs. questions.question: Tuberculosis infection control in a health care facility.

parts.text: List the three levels of control measures that should be included in every infection control program for tuberculosis.

parts_raw.text: List the THREE levels of control measures that should be included in every infection control program for tuberculosis.

questions.model_answer: (1) Administrative (managerial) controls — the most important level: risk assessment, written TB control plan, early identification/triage and isolation of suspect cases, prompt diagnosis and treatment, staff education and TB screening. (2) Environmental (engineering) controls — airborne infection isolation rooms with negative pressure, adequate air changes per hour, HEPA filtration and upper-room UV germicidal irradiation. (3) Personal respiratory protection — fit-tested N95 (or higher) respirators for staff entering the room, within a formal respiratory protection program.
questions.beyond_mandell: Canadian Tuberculosis Standards (TB prevention and control in health care settings): administrative, environmental, personal respiratory protection hierarchy.

questions.question: Tuberculosis infection control in a health care facility.

parts.text: List six specific infection control measures.

parts_raw.text: List SIX specific infection control measures.

questions.model_answer: (1) Triage and screen patients at presentation for cough >2-3 weeks, fever, night sweats and weight loss, with immediate masking of the patient and rapid chest radiography. (2) Place any suspected or confirmed pulmonary/laryngeal TB patient in an airborne infection isolation (negative-pressure) room with at least 6-12 air changes per hour and the door kept closed; keep isolation until three negative AFB smears and clinical improvement on effective therapy (or an alternative diagnosis), and longer for drug-resistant disease. (3) Fit-tested N95 respirators for all staff and visitors entering the room, within a respiratory protection program (medical clearance, fit testing, training, seal check). (4) Prompt collection of sputum for AFB smear, culture and a rapid molecular (NAAT) test, and prompt initiation of effective four-drug therapy with directly observed therapy. (5) Perform cough-inducing/aerosol-generating procedures (sputum induction, bronchoscopy, nebulized therapy, autopsy) only in a negative-pressure room or booth with local exhaust, and minimize patient transport out of the room (surgical mask on the patient when transport is necessary). (6) A health care worker TB screening program with baseline two-step tuberculin skin test or IGRA, periodic testing based on facility risk assessment, contact investigation of unprotected exposures and treatment of latent infection, plus staff and patient education and a written TB control plan with surveillance of conversion rates.
questions.beyond_mandell: Canadian Tuberculosis Standards (TB prevention and control in health care settings).

parts.text: What are three exposure-prone procedures this nurse would no longer be able to perform?
What two criteria may allow her to return to regular duties of possible exposure?

parts_raw.text: What are THREE exposure prone procedures this nurse would no longer be able to perform?

questions.model_answer:
a) Exposure-prone procedures are those in which the worker's gloved hands may be in contact with sharp instruments, needle tips or sharp tissue (bone/teeth) inside a patient's open body cavity, wound or confined anatomic space where the hands or fingertips may not be completely visible at all times. Three examples: (1) open abdominal/pelvic or cardiothoracic surgery with blind or poorly visualized suturing or digital palpation of a needle tip in a body cavity; (2) orthopaedic procedures involving bone fragments or wire/pin fixation; (3) major oral/maxillofacial or dental surgery, or open trauma/vaginal delivery with episiotomy repair, where fingers and a sharp instrument share a confined space. (Assisting at these procedures as scrub nurse — passing and handling sharps within the wound — is the relevant restriction.)
b) (1) Sustained suppression of HIV viral load below the accepted threshold on antiretroviral therapy (undetectable, generally <200 copies/mL) with regular, at least quarterly, monitoring and demonstrated adherence. (2) Formal assessment and ongoing oversight by an expert review panel/occupational health with adherence to recommended practice (double gloving, blunt suture, no-touch technique) — her clinical status and viral load remaining acceptable on serial review.
questions.beyond_mandell: PHAC guidance on health care workers infected with bloodborne viruses / SHEA 2010 guideline: HIV-infected HCWs may perform exposure-prone procedures if viral load is suppressed (<200 copies/mL for HIV in SHEA) with expert panel oversight and regular monitoring.

questions.model_answer:
a) Contact + droplet precautions (RSV/undiagnosed acute respiratory illness in a child). Duration: for the duration of illness — until respiratory symptoms have resolved/are clearly improving and the child is afebrile; young children shed for prolonged periods, so precautions are kept for the admission if symptoms persist rather than stopped at a fixed day count.
b) Routine (standard) precautions with the lesions covered; if the lesions cannot be covered, add contact precautions. Duration: until all lesions are crusted. Airborne precautions are not required for localized dermatomal zoster in an immunocompetent host.
c) Susceptible (unvaccinated, no prior varicella) child: airborne + contact precautions from day 8 to day 21 after first exposure (extend to day 28 if VZIG/VariZIG given). If varicella develops, continue until all lesions are crusted. If immune (2 doses of vaccine, prior disease, or serologically immune): no precautions.
d) Droplet precautions empirically pending diagnosis (add contact precautions in children). Continue for 24 hours after start of effective antimicrobial therapy for Neisseria meningitidis or Haemophilus influenzae type b; discontinue to routine precautions if another bacterial cause (e.g. pneumococcus) or a non-transmissible cause is identified. Enteroviral meningitis in children: contact precautions.

parts.text: What is your advice?

parts_raw.text: What is your advice?

questions.model_answer:
Contact infection prevention and control at both hospitals before any transfer and obtain the outbreak line list, case definitions, and each patient's exposure and symptom status; defer any non-urgent procedure until the outbreaks are declared over.
Ward 6B (influenza unit): transfer only if urgent. On arrival place in droplet + contact precautions in a single room; test for influenza; treat with oseltamivir if symptomatic and give post-exposure oseltamivir prophylaxis if exposed and asymptomatic; maintain precautions for 5 days from symptom onset (longer if immunocompromised); ensure influenza vaccination of patient and staff.
Ward 6A (undiagnosed fever): treat as a potential undiagnosed transmissible illness — single room with empiric droplet + contact precautions (escalate to airborne if a rash or respiratory illness compatible with varicella/measles/TB), investigate the fever, and continue precautions until afebrile 48 hours or a non-transmissible diagnosis is established.
Ward 7C (unaffected): routine practices; no additional precautions.
All three: screen for antibiotic-resistant organisms (MRSA/VRE/ESBL/CRE) on admission as out-of-facility transfers; schedule elective procedures at the end of the list; cohort staff, restrict movement, and notify the OR and receiving units. Offer antiviral prophylaxis to the ward if two or more influenza cases occur within 72 hours on one of your units.

cohort_answer.text: Consult IPAC - discuss with IPAC at the other hospital. parts_raw.text: A) Reuse of tympanostomy blade that is labelled "single use device".

questions.model_answer: Reuse of a single-use device is not acceptable unless it is reprocessed by a licensed third-party reprocessor under Health Canada/FDA regulation; in-house reprocessing of a device labelled single-use should not be done. Key considerations: (1) Spaulding classification — a tympanostomy blade enters sterile tissue and is critical, so it requires sterilization, not disinfection. (2) Device design — can it be fully disassembled, cleaned and all surfaces/lumens accessed, and does the material tolerate cleaning and sterilization without degradation of the cutting edge? (3) Residual bioburden, chemical/endotoxin residue and functional integrity must be validated after each reprocessing cycle, with a defined maximum number of cycles. (4) Regulatory and liability issues — the reprocessor assumes manufacturer responsibility; the original manufacturer's warranty is void. (5) Institutional policy, disclosure/consent, and a cost-benefit assessment versus buying new devices.
questions.beyond_mandell: Health Canada / FDA reprocessed single-use device policy; Spaulding classification.

questions.model_answer:
a) An outbreak is the occurrence of cases of a disease in a defined population in excess of the expected/baseline rate for that place and time (in healthcare, also two or more epidemiologically linked cases of a healthcare-associated infection, or any single case of a never-event/highly transmissible pathogen).

b) (1) Confirm the outbreak exists (compare observed with baseline/endemic rate) and verify the diagnosis. Criteria to release from hospital: DOT arranged; Acceptable tx regimen has been established; Comorbidities/medical conditions have been managed eg HIV; Home isolation is possible while still infectious eg first 2 weeks of tx; Clinical improvement; Drug resistant TB is not suspected
Elements for home isolation: Canadian TB standards
When isolation can be stopped: Suspect TB cases: Airborne precautions may be discontinued if three successive samples of sputum (spontaneous or induced) are negative on smear unless TB is still strongly suspected and no other diagnosis has been made. Confirmed TB cases - Smear negative, culture +, drug susceptible: patient has clinical evidence of improvement + evidence of adherence to at least 2 weeks of effective therapy; may be discharged to home isolation for the period requiring airborne precautions provided there is clinical improvement, drug-resistant TB is not suspected no contraindication for home isolation. Smear positive, culture +, drug susceptible: clinical evidence of improvement, evidence of adherence to at least 2 weeks of effective multidrug therapy based on the known antibiotic sensitivity of the patient's organism, 3 consecutive negative AFB sputum smears, same home isolation criteria. Multi-drug resistant TB cases and those with mono-resistance to rifampin (RMP): should have 3 consecutive negative sputum cultures after six weeks of incubation prior to discontinuing airborne precautions
a. Three essential principles of design: observational; two groups are compared between each other, one with the outcome/disease, the other without the outcome/disease; assess whether there is a statistically significant difference in the rates of exposure to a defined risk factor between the groups
b. Two advantages compared to cohort study: Less expensive, shorter to conduct, requires comparatively few subjects, allows multiple exposures or risk factors to be examined; Allows rare diseases/those with long latency to be examined
c. Statistical measure: Odds ratio

Tocilizumab – antibody to IL-6 receptor used to treat RA. Associated with Herpes Zoster, PJP and atypical mycobacterial infection. Ustekinumab (stelara) – antibody to IL-12 and IL-23 to treat plaque psoriasis. Nothing specific. Belimumab – antibody to B lymphocyte stimulator used to treat SLE. Cocci and CMV pneumonia reported. Abatacept – CTLA-4 Ig blocks CD28 T cell costimulation, used to treat RA. No specific infections risks identified. Belatacept – CTLA-4 IG blocks CD28 costimulation. Associated with PTLD. Natalizumab – inhibits leukocyte chemotaxis, used to treat MS. Associated with PML. Fingolimod – prevents lymphocyte movement out of lymph nodes, used to treat MS. Associated with life threatening herpes virus infections. Anti-TNF – antibodies to TNF or soluble TNF receptor that binds TNF, used to treat RA, IBD etc. Associated with TB. a) Establish immunity - history of varicella/zoster, two documented vaccine doses, or urgent VZV IgG serology. If susceptible, give VariZIG: a seronegative pregnant woman with a significant household exposure is an explicit indication. parts.text: What are the infection prevention and control measures for a surgical case in suspected Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease?

parts_raw.text: What are the IPC measures for a surgical case in suspected CJD?

questions.model_answer: a) Standard precautions suffice for routine patient care; most body fluids including blood can be handled with standard precautions, while special precautions are recommended for handling CSF. For the surgical/neurosurgical setting: (1) Use single-use/disposable instruments wherever practicable to eliminate the need for reprocessing, quarantine, and tracking. (2) Reusable neurosurgical instruments exposed to high-infectivity tissue (brain, spinal cord, dura, posterior eye, pituitary) must be either discarded or decontaminated by prion-specific reprocessing, since routine sterilization does not inactivate prions. (3) Prion-specific reprocessing means prolonged steam autoclaving, or a combination of sodium hydroxide (NaOH) soak followed by autoclaving. (4) The hospital should have guidelines for handling, quarantine, and tracking of instrument sets used on patients biopsied for dementia or undiagnosed neurodegenerative illness, so instruments can be traced and quarantined pending diagnosis.
questions.beyond_mandell: Mandell gives the principle but refers to Chapter 299 for detailed decontamination; the specific CDC/WHO/PHAC protocols (e.g., immersion in 1N NaOH or 20,000 ppm sodium hypochlorite then autoclave at 121°C, incineration of high-infectivity disposables, tissue infectivity categories) come from those guidelines, not this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: CDC/WHO - Disposable material: should be disposed of by incineration if come in contact with high infectivity tissue (brain, cord, eye). Heat-Sensitive material: Soak in 2N NaOH or undiluted sodium hypochlorite for 1 hour then rinse with water. Heat resistant material: if come in contact with high infectivity or low infectivity tissue (CSF, kidneys, lung, liver, lymph nodes, spleen, placenta): Immerse in 1N NaOH and autoclave at 121 C for 30 minutes; rinse, routine sterilization. Immerse in 1N NaOH or bleach (sodium hypochlorite: 20,000 ppm) for 1 hour, then autoclave at 121 C for 1 hour. Clean, then routine sterilization. Repeat step 2. Number of cases documented from instruments: 6. (Notes: Can the instruments tolerate CJD decontamination? if yes, CJD decontaminate & reuse; if no, routine reprocessing separately & quarantine. Is diagnosis of CJD excluded? if yes, reuse; if no, discard.)

parts_raw.text: Provide: 2 resident interventions; 2 staff interventions; 2 environmental interventions; 1 quality assurance intervention; type of curve; attack rate; incubation period; host/pathogen factors influencing spread

questions.model_answer:
a) Residents (2): (1) Contact precautions with single room or cohorting of symptomatic/incontinent residents, dedicated equipment, and exclusion from communal dining and recreational water until resolved; (2) Supervised hand hygiene for residents and counselling to avoid swimming, water activities, and sexual contact while symptomatic.
Staff (2): (1) Reinforced hand hygiene and gloves/gowns for care of symptomatic residents, with strict separation of food-handling from direct care duties; (2) Active identification of ill staff with exclusion of symptomatic staff and food handlers from work until transmission risk is sufficiently reduced per public health criteria.
Environmental (2): (1) Enhanced cleaning/disinfection of washrooms, commodes and high-touch surfaces, with dedicated or disposable equipment; (2) Review of the food service: remove and hold suspect food, correct cooking/holding temperatures, prevent cross-contamination via cutting boards and utensils, and stop any unpasteurized milk or juice.
Quality assurance (1): Formal outbreak investigation — line list and case definition, stool cultures/CIDT with isolates sent for PFGE/WGS subtyping (PulseNet), notification to public health, and audit of hand hygiene and food-handling practice with feedback.
Type of curve: propagated (person-to-person) spread following the initial common-source exposure, indicated by successive case peaks about one incubation period apart across all four units.
Attack rate: number of cases divided by number of residents at risk x 100 (cannot be computed without the denominator on the curve).
Incubation period: about 3 to 4 days (range 1 to 10 days).
Host/pathogen factors: pathogen — very low infectious dose, Shiga toxin 1/2 production (Stx2 strains more virulent) and adherence factors, prolonged faecal shedding; host — advanced age and comorbidity with higher HUS/case fatality (33% in adults 60 years and older), incontinence and cognitive impairment limiting hygiene, gastric acid suppression, and shared communal space/staff.
questions.beyond_mandell: PHAC/CDC enteric outbreak guidance: incubation 3-4 days (range 1-10) and exclusion of cases from food handling/direct care until asymptomatic (often 2 negative stools) are not stated in this chapter.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort calls the curve simply propagated; the chapter's framing supports a common-source outbreak with subsequent propagated person-to-person spread, which is what involvement of all four units implies.

cohort_answer.text: Resident: isolation of those with symptoms; handwashing. Staff: increased hand washing; using proper PPE. Environmental: single person bathrooms; disinfection of rooms. QA: investigation/tracking of cases. Type of curve: propagated. Attack rate/incubation period: can't calculate without the curve. Host/pathogen factors: host susceptibility; basic reproductive number/infectivity.

questions.model_answer:
a) An outbreak is the occurrence of cases of a disease in a defined population, place and time period in excess of the expected/baseline number; in a healthcare setting a cluster of epidemiologically linked cases (often two or more) of a healthcare-associated infection above baseline, or even a single case of a never-event pathogen (e.g. hospital-acquired Legionella or group A streptococcus).
b) (1) Verify the diagnosis and confirm that a true excess over baseline exists. (2) Establish a working case definition (person, place, time, clinical/lab criteria) and actively case-find. (3) Line-list cases and construct an epidemic curve; describe by time, place and person. (4) Institute immediate control measures — appropriate additional precautions, cohorting, unit/admission restriction, enhanced cleaning, staff exclusion — and notify IPAC, administration and public health while assembling the outbreak management team.
c) (1) Sodium hypochlorite (bleach) 1000-5000 ppm available chlorine. (2) Accelerated hydrogen peroxide (or another virucidal agent with a demonstrated non-enveloped virus claim, e.g. hydrogen peroxide vapour); alcohol-based hand rub is NOT reliably effective — use soap and water.

questions.model_answer: a) Routine/standard precautions – no person-to-person transmission. b) Biosafety Level 2 practices suffice for handling yeast-phase clinical specimens; Biosafety Level 3 is required when propagating the sporulating mould phase or processing soil, with mould-phase work done in a biological safety cabinet. c) By inhalation of microconidia aerosolized from bird/bat guano-enriched soil that has been disturbed, or from sporulating mould cultures in the laboratory. d) (1) Immunosuppression (transplant recipient), at risk of progressive disseminated disease. (2) Failure to improve after >1 month of illness or hypoxemia.
questions.beyond_mandell: BSL-2 for yeast-phase specimen handling reflects standard laboratory biosafety guidance; Mandell text explicitly states only that mycelial-phase manipulation requires BSL-3. Immunosuppression as a treatment indication is IDSA-based.

cohort_answer.text: Nurse: Routine practices. Lab technician: Laboratory Safety and Containment - infective stage (conidia) present in sporulating mold form cultures and soil from endemic areas; yeast form in tissues/fluids may cause local infection via parenteral inoculation or mucous membrane splash; BSL-2/ABSL-2 practices recommended for handling/processing clinical specimens, identifying isolates, animal tissues, mold cultures (any culture identifying dimorphic fungi handled in Class II BSC); BSL-3 practices for propagating sporulating cultures in mold form or processing soil/environmental materials likely to contain infectious conidia. Summary: BSL2 minimum for yeast-form specimens, BSL3 when propagating spores in mold/soil. Acquisition: grows in soil enriched with guano from avian species/bats; spores circulate in air after soil disturbed; acquired through inhalation of spores; once inhaled, converts to yeast form due to body temp, activates inflammatory cascade, travels to lymph nodes to spread. Indications to treat: acute pulmonary histo if symptoms not better after >1 month of illness or hypoxemia (most people with acute pulm histo don't need therapy, just bed rest+antipyretics); cavitary pulmonary histo (progressive loss of pulmonary function without treatment); acute disseminated histo; histo-related meningitis and endocarditis. Do not need to treat: pericarditis, arthropathies (treat with NSAIDs +/- steroids); hilar/mediastinal lymphadenopathy from acute pulmonary histo (treat if persistent). Definite indications (proven/probable efficacy): acute diffuse pulmonary infection moderate-severe symptoms; chronic cavitary pulmonary infection; progressive disseminated infection; CNS infection. Uncertain indication: acute focal pulmonary infection, asymptomatic or mild symptoms persisting >1 month; mediastinal lymphadenitis; mediastinal granuloma; inflammatory syndromes treated with corticosteroids. Not recommended: mediastinal fibrosis; pulmonary nodule; broncholithiasis; presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome.

questions.model_answer:
a) Residents: (1) Place symptomatic residents on contact precautions in a single room with dedicated toileting/commode, and cohort cases if single rooms are unavailable. (2) Restrict movement — cancel group dining and group activities, restrict transfers and new admissions to the affected unit, and supervise resident hand hygiene before meals and after toileting.
Staff: (1) Cohort staff to affected versus unaffected residents, with hand hygiene using soap and water and gowns/gloves for all contact; (2) exclude symptomatic staff from work until asymptomatic (and screen/culture them), with education and no food handling while ill.
Environment: enhanced cleaning and disinfection of high-touch surfaces, bathrooms and commodes with an appropriate disinfectant at increased frequency, and review food handling/water source with removal of any implicated food.
b) (1) Confirm the outbreak exists and verify the diagnosis (compare with baseline; confirm isolates, consider molecular typing). (2) Establish a case definition and find cases systematically (line list by person, place, time; draw the epidemic curve). (3) Generate and test hypotheses about the source and mode of transmission (cohort or case-control study, environmental/food sampling). (4) Implement control measures and communicate/report findings to public health, then monitor for further cases and declare the outbreak over.
c) Host factor: susceptible elderly residents with immunosenescence, incontinence and dependence on staff for personal care, permitting ongoing person-to-person transmission (a propagated outbreak with successive generations of cases). Pathogen factor: a very low infectious dose with an incubation period of about 3-4 days, so cases cluster one incubation period apart — the q4d peaks correspond to successive generations of transmission rather than a point source.

C. haemulonii is a common misidentification of C. auris by older biochemical/automated platforms, and C. auris is an emerging multidrug-resistant yeast that is highly transmissible in healthcare settings and causes invasive disease with high mortality.
